objectives: Survey main-group chemistry of H, N, halogens, noble gases, B clusters, silicones, FLPs.
Understand f-block — lanthanide vs actinide chemistry, 4f vs 5f, magnetic + luminescence properties.
Cover nuclear inorganic chemistry — radioactivity, half-lives, fission/fusion, transuranium synthesis.

slides.title: Main-group: H, N, halogens, noble gases, boron clusters, silicones, FLPs
slides.body:
**Hydrogen** (H, Z=1): unique — sometimes classified group 1 (alkali-like H⁺), sometimes group 17 (halogen-like H⁻). Three isotopes: ¹H (99.985%), ²D (deuterium, 0.015%), ³T (tritium, radioactive, β⁻, t₁/₂ = 12.3 yr). H₂ bond energy 436 kJ/mol; smallest molecule.
- **Industrial production**: steam reforming CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂; water-gas shift CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂; chlor-alkali electrolysis. Annual production ~90 million tons.
- **Green hydrogen**: electrolysis from renewable electricity; central to decarbonization strategy.
- **Hydrogen economy**: storage (compressed, liquefied, metal hydrides LaNi₅H₆, NaBH₄, MOFs), fuel cells (PEM, SOFC), Haber-Bosch ammonia, methanol synthesis, hydrocracking.

**Nitrogen** (N, Z=7): N≡N triple bond (944 kJ/mol — among the strongest). Atmosphere 78% N₂.
- **Fixed nitrogen**: biological (nitrogenase Mo-Fe + V-Fe + Fe-only enzymes; ~half global fixation) + industrial (Haber-Bosch ~half).
- **Inorganic nitrogen compounds**: NH₃ (basic, Brønsted-Lowry); HNO₃ (strong acid, Ostwald process); HNO₂; NO + NO₂ (atmospheric chemistry — smog + ozone destruction); N₂O₃ + N₂O₄ + N₂O₅; hydrazine N₂H₄ (rocket fuel); HN₃ + azides (explosive).
- **Nitrogen oxides + Lewis structures**: NO (radical, biological signaling — Furchgott-Ignarro-Murad Nobel 1998 nitric oxide as signaling molecule).

**Halogens** (F, Cl, Br, I, At): group 17, 7 valence electrons, oxidizing.
- **Activity**: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. F is most electronegative element (Pauling 4.0). F₂ so reactive it attacks every element except some noble gases + Ne; isolated in 1886 by Moissan (Nobel 1906).
- **Interhalogens**: ClF, BrF₃, IF₅, IF₇, ICl₃, etc. IF₇ pentagonal bipyramidal.
- **Polyhalides**: I₃⁻ (linear, in iodine starch test), I₅⁻, I₇⁻.
- **Halates + perhalates**: HClO (hypo), HClO₂ (chlorous), HClO₃ (chloric), HClO₄ (perchloric). pK_a's span ~10 across the series.
- **Acid + base strength of HX**: HF (pK_a 3.2, weak due to strong H-F bond), HCl (-7), HBr (-9), HI (-10).

**Noble gases** (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og): group 18, full ns²np⁶.
- Long thought inert; **Bartlett 1962** synthesized XePtF₆ — first noble-gas compound. Triggered an explosion of noble-gas chemistry.
- **Xenon compounds**: XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeO₄, XeOF₄. Mostly with F (most electronegative). Xe + Kr more reactive; He + Ne + Ar largely inert (some HArF in matrix isolation).
- Bartlett's discovery overturned chemistry dogma; opened Group 18 chemistry.

**Boron + boranes + carboranes** (Lipscomb Nobel 1976):
- Boron: B(III) electron-deficient, 3 valence e⁻ → forms 3-center-2-electron bonds (3c-2e).
- **Boranes** (Stock 1912+): B₂H₆ (diborane), B₅H₉, B₆H₁₀, B₁₀H₁₄, B₁₂H₁₂²⁻ (icosahedral, aromatic), B₂₀H₁₈²⁻.
- **Wade's rules**: predict cluster geometry from electron counting. closo (n+1 SEPs), nido (n+2), arachno (n+3), hypho (n+4).
- **Carboranes**: C₂B₁₀H₁₂ (icosahedral, very stable), ortho/meta/para isomers — used in BNCT (boron neutron capture therapy for cancer), polymers, catalysis.
- **Lipscomb (Nobel 1976)**: 'studies on the structure of boranes illuminating problems of chemical bonding'.

**Silicones**: polymers with $\text{R}_2\text{SiO}$ repeat — Si-O backbones with organic R substituents. PDMS (polydimethylsiloxane) ubiquitous: lubricants, sealants, biomedical implants, breast implants, contact lenses, microfluidics chips. Discovered by Frederick Kipping 1900s; Dow Corning industrialized.

**Frustrated Lewis Pairs (FLPs)** (Douglas Stephan 2006 + Gerhard Erker, ongoing): bulky Lewis acid + bulky Lewis base that cannot combine due to steric hindrance, but cooperate to activate small molecules (H₂, CO₂, N₂O, NH₃).
- $(\text{Mes})_3\text{P} + \text{B(C}_6\text{F}_5)_3 \to$ heterolytic H₂ activation → metal-free hydrogenation.
- Major theme in modern inorganic + catalysis: replace expensive transition metal catalysts with main-group cooperative catalysis.
- CO₂ + N₂O activation by FLPs; main-group catalytic cycles competitive with TM.

slides.title: f-block: lanthanides + actinides — 4f vs 5f, magnetic + luminescence
slides.body:
**f-block elements** (4f lanthanides Ce-Lu; 5f actinides Th-Lr): 14 elements per row inserted between groups 2 + 3 in periods 6 + 7.

**Lanthanides** (Ce, Z=58 → Lu, Z=71; also La + Y by extension): 4f orbitals.
- **4f orbitals contracted** (relativistic + screening): essentially core-like, poorly involved in bonding. Chemistry dominated by 6s² + 5d⁰⁻¹.
- **Common oxidation state +3**: Ln³⁺ = [Xe]4f^n; ionic radii decrease across series (lanthanide contraction).
- **Less common**: Ce(IV) (4f⁰, like Hf), Eu(II) + Yb(II) (4f⁷ + 4f¹⁴ stable half/full f shell).
- **Magnetic properties**: Ln³⁺ paramagnetic with large magnetic moments (4f electrons unquenched orbital momentum; SOC strong → use $\mu_{eff} = g_J \sqrt{J(J+1)}$). Curie-Weiss behavior.
- **Luminescence**: f-f transitions are Laporte-forbidden + spin-forbidden → sharp emission lines (atomic-like) + long lifetimes (ms scale). Used in: lasers (Nd:YAG 1064 nm, Er-doped fiber amplifiers for telecom, Yb:YAG ultrafast), phosphors (Y₂O₃:Eu³⁺ red, LaPO₄:Ce,Tb green, BaMgAl₁₀O₁₇:Eu²⁺ blue for fluorescent + LED lighting), MRI contrast (Gd³⁺-DTPA + Gd-DOTA), upconversion nanoparticles (NaYF₄:Yb,Er for bioimaging), euros (Eu² + Eu³ phosphor security).
- **Industrial**: Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets (strongest, in wind turbines + EV motors + speakers + hard drives); Tb + Dy for high-T magnet applications; misch metal (Ce-La-Nd-Pr alloy) for lighter flints + catalytic converters (Ce₂O₃ oxygen storage). Most rare earths from China (~85% mining); supply-chain strategic concern. **Rare earths are misnomers** — Ce (cerium) is more abundant than Cu.

**Actinides** (Ac, Z=89 → Lr, Z=103): 5f orbitals.
- **5f orbitals more diffuse** than 4f → involved in bonding → wider range of oxidation states.
- Early actinides (Th, Pa, U, Np, Pu) show OS +3 to +7. U(VI) common (UO₂²⁺ uranyl); important for nuclear fuel.
- **Heavy actinides** (Am, Cm onward): behave more like lanthanides — 5f becomes core-like.
- **Naturally occurring**: U-235 (0.72%), U-238 (99.27%), U-234 trace; Th-232; Ac, Pa from U decay.
- **Transuranium elements** (Z > 92): synthetic. Np + Pu (Seaborg + McMillan 1940s, Nobel 1951); Am + Cm + Bk + Cf + Es + Fm + Md + No + Lr (Berkeley/Seaborg group + others).
- **Glenn T. Seaborg**: identified ~10 transuranium elements; proposed the **actinide concept** (1944) restructuring periodic table to include f-block; Nobel 1951 (with McMillan). Element 106 named seaborgium (Sg).

**Lanthanide vs actinide chemistry**:
- Both have +3 as common OS for trivalent ions; ionic radii similar after contraction.
- Actinides more redox-active (multiple OS); more covalent due to 5f extension.
- Magnetic + luminescent: lanthanides better-behaved (sharp f-f transitions, predictable g_J); actinides messier (SOC + 5f delocalization).
- **Single-molecule magnets** (SMMs): mononuclear lanthanide complexes (e.g., DyClA, TbPc₂, Dy bisamido) show magnetic memory at low T due to ground-state anisotropy. Latest blocking temperature record: ~80 K for Dy metallocene (Layfield + Mills + Tong 2018 onward); approaching practical magnetic-data-storage temperature regime.

**Lanthanide complexes in biology + medicine**: Gd-DTPA + Gd-DOTA contrast agents (annual ~50M doses); europium- + terbium-based luminescent probes for bioimaging; lanthanide-tagged antibodies for mass cytometry (CyTOF, Fluidigm). **Lanthanide-toxicity concerns**: Gd retention in brain tissue (after >100 contrast injections) is now FDA-monitored.

slides.title: Nuclear inorganic: radioactivity, half-lives, neutron capture, fission/fusion, transuranium synthesis
slides.body:
**Nuclear chemistry**: studies properties + reactions of atomic nuclei — radioactive decay, fission, fusion, neutron capture, transuranium synthesis. Foundational to nuclear power, medical isotopes, dating, nuclear weapons history.

**Radioactive decay modes**:
- **α (alpha)**: ⁴He²⁺ nucleus emitted; mass number -4, atomic number -2. Heavy elements (Th, U, Pu); high ionization + low penetration; stopped by paper.
- **β⁻ (beta minus)**: neutron → proton + e⁻ + ν̄_e; atomic number +1; common in neutron-rich isotopes (³H, ¹⁴C, ³²P, ⁹⁰Sr, ¹³¹I).
- **β⁺ (beta plus, positron)**: proton → neutron + e⁺ + ν_e; atomic number -1; proton-rich isotopes (¹⁸F for PET).
- **EC (electron capture)**: inner-shell e⁻ + p → n + ν; A unchanged, Z decreases. ⁵¹Cr, ⁵⁷Co, ⁵⁵Fe, ¹²⁵I.
- **γ (gamma)**: excited nuclear state emits photon; no change in A or Z. Often follows other decays.
- **Spontaneous fission**: very heavy nuclei (²⁵²Cf, ²⁴⁴Cm) split into two fragments + neutrons.
- **IT (isomeric transition)**: metastable nuclear state decays to ground state via γ. ⁹⁹ᵐTc → ⁹⁹Tc + γ (140 keV).

**Half-life** $t_{1/2}$: time for half a sample to decay. First-order kinetics:
$$ N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}; \quad t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda $$
Ranges from microseconds (²¹⁰Po α-emitter t₁/₂ = 138 d, but very heavy nuclei < ms) to billions of years (²³⁸U 4.47 Gyr, ⁴⁰K 1.25 Gyr).

**Radioactive dating**:
- **Carbon-14**: ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio in atmosphere ~1.3 × 10⁻¹². Living things equilibrate; dead organisms decay (t₁/₂ = 5730 yr). Range ~50000 yr. Libby Nobel 1960.
- **Uranium-lead** (²³⁸U → ²⁰⁶Pb, ²³⁵U → ²⁰⁷Pb): zircon (ZrSiO₄ + U) - rich; range to >4.5 Gyr; established age of Earth ~4.54 Gyr.
- **K-Ar** (⁴⁰K → ⁴⁰Ar): dating volcanic rocks 100 kyr – Gyr range.
- **Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, Re-Os**: long-lived geochronology + isotope geochemistry tools.

**Neutron capture** $(n, \gamma)$: nucleus absorbs neutron + emits gamma; A increases by 1. Used in: nuclear-reactor breeding (²³⁸U + n → ²³⁹Pu via β⁻); isotope production (⁵⁹Co + n → ⁶⁰Co for radiotherapy + sterilization); s-process + r-process stellar nucleosynthesis (origins of heavy elements; r-process in neutron-star mergers — LIGO/Virgo confirmed kilonova 2017).

**Nuclear fission**: heavy nucleus + neutron → two medium-mass fragments + 2-3 neutrons + ~200 MeV.
- $^{235}\text{U} + n \to ^{141}\text{Ba} + ^{92}\text{Kr} + 3n + 200$ MeV (Hahn + Strassmann 1938; Meitner + Frisch interpretation 1939).
- Chain reaction → uncontrolled (bomb) or controlled (reactor).
- Reactor types: PWR + BWR (light-water), CANDU (heavy-water), graphite-moderated (Chernobyl RBMK, weapons reactors), GCR (gas-cooled), MSR (molten salt — re-emerging), fast breeder (sodium-cooled).
- Fuel cycle: U enrichment (gas centrifuge for ²³⁵U from 0.72% to 3-5% LEU + >90% HEU for weapons), fuel fabrication, irradiation, reprocessing (PUREX for Pu + U), waste storage.
- Decay chains: ²³⁵U → ²³¹Th → ... → ²⁰⁷Pb (4 chains naturally).

**Nuclear fusion**: light nuclei combine → ~MeV per nucleon. Solar energy. Engineered: D-T tokamak (ITER under construction in France, demonstrating energy gain Q > 10; NIF Lawrence Livermore National Ignition Facility ignition Dec 2022 — first net gain Q > 1 at the target). Commercial fusion: SPARC + ARC (Commonwealth Fusion Systems + MIT) + Tokamak Energy + General Fusion + TAE Technologies + Helion + Zap Energy + etc. — 'startup era' for fusion.

**Transuranium synthesis**:
- **Neutron capture (slow)**: ²³⁸U + n → ²³⁹U → β⁻ → ²³⁹Np → β⁻ → ²³⁹Pu. Industrial Pu from reactors.
- **Heavy-ion bombardment**: target nucleus + accelerated heavy ion → fused superheavy nucleus + neutrons. ²⁰⁸Pb + ⁶⁴Ni → ²⁷¹Ds; ²⁴⁹Bk + ⁵⁰Ti → ²⁹⁴Ts.
- Berkeley + Dubna + GSI (Darmstadt) + RIKEN (Wakō, Japan) labs.
- Elements 113-118: Nh, Fl, Mc, Lv, Ts, Og (named 2016). Element 117 (tennessine) from Oak Ridge + ORNL + Dubna; element 113 (nihonium) from RIKEN.
- **Island of stability** prediction: doubly magic ²⁹⁸Fl (N=184, Z=114)? Half-lives may rise from ms to years. Not yet experimentally accessed.

**Medical isotopes** (huge market, ~50M procedures/yr):
- **Diagnostic γ-emitters**: ⁹⁹ᵐTc (most-used, ~85% of nuclear medicine), ¹²³I, ¹³¹I, ²⁰¹Tl, ⁶⁷Ga.
- **PET (β⁺)**: ¹⁸F (FDG most common), ¹¹C, ¹⁵O, ⁶⁸Ga, ⁸⁹Zr, ⁶⁴Cu.
- **Therapeutic β⁻**: ⁹⁰Y, ¹⁷⁷Lu, ¹³¹I, ¹⁸⁶Re, ¹⁸⁸Re.
- **Targeted α therapy**: ²²⁵Ac, ²¹³Bi, ²¹¹At — short range α tracks, devastating to cells; growing area in oncology (Ra-223 first FDA TAT 2013 for bone-metastatic prostate cancer; Lu-177 PSMA + Ac-225 PSMA in clinical trials).

question.question: Compute the age of a sample by ¹⁴C dating
question.goal: A wood sample has ¹⁴C activity 8.5 disintegrations per minute (dpm)/g of carbon. Living carbon: 13.6 dpm/g. ¹⁴C half-life: 5730 yr. Compute the age.

steps.prompt: Write the first-order decay equation in terms of activity ratio.
steps.reveal: $A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ where λ = decay constant. Take ln: $\lambda t = \ln(A_0/A)$; $t = (1/\lambda) \ln(A_0/A)$.

steps.prompt: Compute decay constant from half-life: $\lambda = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$.

steps.reveal: $t = 0.47 / (1.21 \times 10^{-4}) \approx 3886 \approx 3900 \text{ yr}$ before present. **Libby (Nobel 1960)** established ¹⁴C dating; underpins archaeology, paleoclimatology, art authentication. Calibration via dendrochronology + speleothems + corals + ice cores corrects for atmospheric ¹⁴C variation (Suess wiggles, bomb spike post-1950). Modern AMS (accelerator mass spectrometry) extends practical range to ~50000 yr.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{t = \frac{t_{1/2}}{\ln 2}\ln(A_0/A) \approx 3900 \text{ yr}}$$ ¹⁴C dating: living carbon equilibrates with atmospheric ratio ~1.3 × 10⁻¹²; after death no replenishment; first-order decay. Range ~300-50000 yr. Foundational tool in archaeology + paleoclimatology + forensic + art authentication. Libby Nobel 1960. Modern AMS far surpasses original gas-counting techniques.

question.question: Why was Neil Bartlett's 1962 synthesis of XePtF₆ such a revolutionary discovery?
options: **Overturned the dogma that noble gases are entirely unreactive**. Until 1962, every undergraduate text taught that noble gases (Group 18) had closed-shell ns²np⁶ configurations rendering them chemically inert — useful as inert atmospheres but not partners in compounds. Bartlett, working with PtF₆ (a very strong oxidizer — he had noticed it oxidized O₂ to O₂⁺PtF₆⁻), reasoned that Xe (ionization energy 1170 kJ/mol) is similar to O₂ (1175 kJ/mol). He combined PtF₆ + Xe → red solid XePtF₆ (later shown to be XeFPtF₆ or [XeF]⁺[Pt₂F₁₁]⁻ depending on conditions). Bartlett's prediction-by-analogy + bench-top demonstration opened **Group 18 chemistry**: XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeO₄, XeOF₄, XeOF₂; later KrF₂, RnF₂; even matrix-isolated HArF (Räsänen 2000). Lessons: (1) periodic trends are still predictive at the edges; (2) 'inert' is an empirical observation, not a thermodynamic law; (3) high-OS fluorides + oxygen fluorides are key access to unusual chemistry. Bartlett's work + the subsequent noble-gas chemistry research community (Christe, Holloway, Pyykkö) established a new field. Aside: ⁸⁵Kr + ¹³³Xe noble-gas radioactivity provided early atmospheric tracer; current noble-gas geochemistry uses ³He + ⁴He + ²⁰⁻²²Ne + ³⁶,³⁸,⁴⁰Ar isotopes to trace fluid flow + age + nucleosynthesis.
question.explanation: Bartlett 1962: XePtF₆ overturned 'inert gas' dogma. Reasoning: Xe IE ≈ O₂ IE; PtF₆ oxidizes O₂ → Xe should also. Birth of Group 18 chemistry: XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeOF₂, etc. Even KrF₂ + matrix HArF. Lesson: periodic trends + Lewis acid-base + redox extend into ostensibly 'inert' regions.

hints: What did people think about noble gases before 1962?
slides.workedSolution: Bartlett 1962 synthesized XePtF₆ by analogy: Xe IE (1170 kJ/mol) ≈ O₂ IE (1175 kJ/mol); PtF₆ oxidizes O₂; therefore should oxidize Xe. Opened Group 18 chemistry (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃, etc.; KrF₂; HArF). Overturned 'inert gas' dogma; periodic trends + redox extend into entire periodic table.

question.question: Lanthanide single-molecule magnets
question.prompt: Mononuclear Dy(III) bisamido + dysprosocene complexes (Layfield, Mills, Tong, McInnes ~2018+) achieve magnetic blocking temperatures > 60-80 K — the highest yet for single-molecule magnets. (a) Why are Dy(III) (4f⁹) + Tb(III) (4f⁸) particularly favorable for SMM design, and what role do unquenched orbital angular momentum + strong spin-orbit coupling + crystal-field anisotropy play? (b) How does the magnetic blocking temperature relate to potential applications in quantum information + ultra-high-density data storage? (c) Why hasn't anyone reached room-temperature SMM behavior yet, and what design principles might bridge the gap?

question.question: ²³⁹Pu has a half-life of 24100 years. What fraction of a sample remains after 100000 years? Compute to 4 decimals.
question.hint: N/N₀ = (1/2)^(t/t₁/₂) = (1/2)^(100000/24100) = (1/2)^4.149 = 2^(-4.149) ≈ 0.0561. After ~4.15 half-lives, ~5.6% of original Pu remains. Why nuclear waste storage requires ~100,000 yr containment.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain how main-group inorganic chemistry (H, N, halogens, noble gases, B clusters, FLPs) connects to f-block (lanthanides + actinides) + nuclear chemistry, and how all three subfields shape modern technology + medicine.
question.rubric: Mentions: main group — H + N (Haber-Bosch + green ammonia); halogens (F most reactive, HF + interhalogens); noble gases (Bartlett 1962 XePtF₆ overturning inert dogma); boron clusters (Lipscomb Nobel 1976 + carboranes + BNCT); silicones (Kipping); frustrated Lewis pairs (Stephan-Erker 2006+ metal-free H₂ activation). f-block — lanthanides (4f core-like, +3 OS, sharp f-f emission used in lasers + phosphors + MRI Gd-DTPA + Nd-Fe-B magnets) vs actinides (5f more bonding, multiple OS, Pu in reactors). Glenn Seaborg (Nobel 1951) actinide concept + 10 transuranium elements. Nuclear chemistry: α/β/γ decay; ¹⁴C dating (Libby Nobel 1960); U-Pb geochronology; fission (Hahn-Meitner 1938-39); fusion (NIF ignition 2022, ITER); medical isotopes (⁹⁹ᵐTc, ¹⁸F-FDG, ¹⁷⁷Lu + ²²⁵Ac targeted α therapy). Conclude: main-group + f-block + nuclear together cover the breadth of elements + isotopes powering pharma + energy + materials + cosmology.
